solver: LS-DYNA R13.1 MPP (double precision), INSA Rennes cluster

examples.title: Concrete cylinder 150 × 300 mm — uniaxial compression
setup: Full cylinder, O-grid mesh of 16 000 hexahedra (≈ 7.5 mm), ELFORM 1 with Flanagan–Belytschko stiffness hourglass control (IHQ 4, QM 0.05).

Bottom face fixed in z; one centre node and one edge node fix rigid-body motion. Top face pushed down 3 mm (1 % strain) in 30 ms with a 0.5 ms smooth start. Platens are frictionless, so the stress state is uniaxial.
Stress = bottom reaction / (π · 75²); strain = platen displacement / 300 mm.
Every material card is the site's generator output for f_c = 30 MPa (mean cylinder strength), d_max = 16 mm, ρ = 2.3 t/m³. The KCC card is regularised for its 7.5 mm elements.
notes: With rate effects off, KCC, CSCM and CDP peak at 30.2, 30.2 and 30.0 MPa: the generated cards reproduce the input f_c within 1 %. The initial modulus of CSCM and CDP is 30–32 GPa, close to the EN 1992-1-1 value E_cm = 22 (f_cm/10)^0.3 ≈ 30.6 GPa. KCC starts at 25.8 GPa: since generator version 1.5 its EOS follows the ACI relation E = 57 000 √f_c (psi) on which the K&C fit is based.

KCC with its DIF curve peaks at 42.6 MPa (+41 %). The explicit test runs at about 0.3–1 s⁻¹, where the CEB-FIP MC90 compressive DIF for f_c = 30 MPa is 1.34–1.40, so the solver is doing what the curve asks. For quasi-static analyses set dif_model = 0 (LCRATE = 0), or use the lower fib MC2010 curve (dif_model = 2).

Post-peak behaviour differs widely at 1 % strain: CDP keeps 43 % of its peak, KCC 84 %, CSCM 91 %. With frictionless platens the strain field stays nearly uniform, so these branches are mostly a material response. They depend on the compressive softening parameters (EFC for CDP, GFC for CSCM, b1 and the λ–η curve for KCC). The KCC branch is more ductile than with a fixed λ–η curve because the generator stretches the softening to the element size.

Winfrith reaches f_c correctly (30.0–30.7 MPa up to 2.5 ‰ with every hourglass setting), but its curve after about 3 ‰ is decided by the hourglass control, not by the material. With the same card and mesh, IHQ 4 / QM 0.05 climbs to 42 MPa, IHQ 6 to 35 MPa, IHQ 4 / QM 0.01 peaks at 34 MPa and drops to 19 MPa, and viscous IHQ 1 collapses to 1 MPa. A single element under the same loading stays at 30.4 MPa, so the card itself is not the cause.

Why: in the cylinder, vertical splitting cracks soften the elements laterally, and the one-point element then deforms in hourglass modes (the shaft pinches in, tilts or collapses in a band, see the plots). The axial element stresses stay at about 30 MPa or less and the lateral stress near zero, so the extra load with IHQ 4 is carried by hourglass forces, not by confinement. Winfrith exists only for ELFORM 1: LS-DYNA R13 switches ELFORM 2 back to 1 (Warning 20101), so a fully integrated element is not an option. Use Winfrith where tensile cracking governs, and do not trust its compressive post-peak branch; if you must, compare at least two hourglass settings.

Hourglass energy stays below 0.5 % of the external work for KCC, CSCM and CDP, and kinetic energy below 0.6 %. For Winfrith the total (0.9 % with IHQ 4, 5–7 % with the other settings) hides the problem: with IHQ 4 it stays near 0.1 % of the work up to 20 ms, then grows by about 5 % of the work done in the last 3 ms, exactly where the load climbs.

examples.title: Notched concrete prism 150 × 150 × 550 mm — three-point bending
setup: EN 14651 geometry: span 500 mm, central notch 25 mm deep and one element (4.95 mm) wide. 99 750 hexahedra of ≈ 5 mm, fully integrated (ELFORM 2). A first run with ELFORM 1 + hourglass control lost 20–55 % of the external work to hourglass energy once the crack localised, so it was discarded.
Supports and loading line are rows of nodes (three node lines at each support, two at midspan). Midspan pushed down 1 mm in 40 ms.
CMOD is the opening of the two bottom nodes at the notch edges. GF = work of the load over the deflection / ligament area (125 × 150 mm²), without the self-weight correction.
f_ct,L uses EN 14651: 3 F_L l / (2 b h_sp²), with F_L the largest load for CMOD ≤ 0.05 mm.
KCC is run without the DIF curve so that all four models are compared quasi-statically. Its card is regularised for the 5 mm elements (generator input elm_size = 5).
notes: CDP is the reference here: its bilinear softening law (FT 2.36, FT1 0.71 MPa, WF1 0.038, WF 0.254 mm) encloses the fib MC2010 value 0.135 N/mm, and the test returns 0.134 N/mm. CDP defines softening as stress versus crack opening and scales it by the element length internally, so the dissipated energy matches the card.

KCC dissipates 0.114 N/mm, about 2.4 times the 0.048 N/mm of the unregularised card, and f_ct,L rises from 2.9 to 3.7 MPa. The generator stretches the post-peak λ points so that one 5 mm element in uniaxial tension dissipates 0.135 N/mm; in the beam the crack band spreads over three to four elements and the measured G_F is about 15 % below that target. Up to generator version 1.5 (b2 from the K&C formula) the same beam gave 0.096 N/mm and 3.4 MPa. See the KCC documentation.

Winfrith and CSCM dissipate more than their cards ask for: 0.109 vs 0.064 N/mm (×1.7) and 0.094 vs GFT 0.064 N/mm (×1.5). With RATE = 1, Winfrith's FE is the crack opening at zero stress, w_c = 2 G_F / UTS = 0.054 mm, so its card G_F is 0.064 N/mm, the same value the CSCM generator writes. With the EN 1992-1-1 tensile strength (f_ctm = 2.36 MPa for f_cm = 30 MPa) they give f_ct,L = 3.9 and 4.0 MPa, CDP 3.9 MPa and KCC 3.7 MPa. Calibrate G_F for Winfrith and CSCM against a test like this one rather than trusting the input value.

The crack runs straight up from the notch tip in all models. CSCM erodes the cracked elements (ERODE = 1.05), which shows as a gap in the fringe plot; the other models keep the elements and localise the strain.

With ELFORM 2 the hourglass energy is zero for KCC, CSCM and CDP. Winfrith is implemented only in the one-point element (the manual says ELFORM = 1), so it keeps hourglass modes and reports 5.9 % hourglass energy. Kinetic energy stays below 0.5 % of the external work, so the 40 ms loading is quasi-static.

examples.title: Round steel bar d₀ = 10 mm — tensile test (ISO 6892-1 proportional specimen)
setup: Parallel length 80 mm, gauge L₀ = 50 mm = 5.65 √S₀. O-grid mesh of 8 000 hexahedra (≈ 1 mm), ELFORM 2. The diameter is reduced by 0.5 % at mid-length, so the neck forms in the gauge length.
One end fixed, the other pulled 24 mm in 60 ms (about 5 s⁻¹ in the gauge length). Mass scaling to Δt = 1E-4 ms affects only the smallest elements.
Engineering stress = reaction / (π · 5²); engineering strain = change in the gauge length / 50 mm.

All three models describe the same S355 steel: MAT_024 uses the Yun & Gardner (2017) curve for f_y = 355 and f_u = 510 MPa, extended beyond A_g with slope H = σ_true(A_g), the Considère criterion at A_g (generator v1.2). The fracture run adds FAIL = 1.01, the generator value for Z = 59 % (BAM S355) and 1 mm elements. MAT_003 (SIGY 355.6, ETAN 1646) and MAT_015 (A 355.6, B 1137, n 0.822, C 0) are least-squares fits to that curve, made for this example.
notes: All three fits start yielding at 351–353 MPa at 0.2 % strain, so the elastic–plastic transition is consistent.

MAT_024 with the Yun & Gardner curve gives R_m = 504 MPa (input f_u = 510) at A_g = 18.7 % (Yun & Gardner predict 18.2 %). The neck forms at the reduced section and the load then drops gradually, as in a real test. With the flat tail of generator v1.1 the neck formed earlier (A_g = 17.9 %) and thinned faster.

MAT_003 (bilinear) and MAT_015 (Johnson–Cook) never neck within 30 % strain: their hardening stays above the Considère criterion (dσ/dε ≥ σ), so the engineering stress keeps rising to 606 and 546 MPa. A least-squares fit that matches the curve well up to f_u still over-predicts strength beyond it. Use MAT_024 with a measured true-stress curve when necking or ductile failure matters, or fit MAT_003/MAT_015 only up to A_g and add a failure criterion.

Without FAIL the neck thins without fracture. With FAIL from Z = 59 % the bar breaks at 35.5 % engineering strain, close to the A = 35 % of the BAM flat specimens with the same Z (next example). The values of round and flat specimens are not strictly comparable: A depends on the gauge length and the section shape. The free ends ring after fracture, so the curve is cut there.

examples.title: S355 flat specimen 6 × 20 mm — tensile test to fracture against BAM test data
setup: Test data: BAM tensile tests on S355 plate, specimens Zx2–Zx4 (Zenodo record 6778336, CC BY 4.0). Flat specimens a × b = 6 × 20 mm, gauge L0 = 60 mm. The protocol gives A = 35 % and Z = 58–61 % for all three.

One eighth of the specimen with symmetry planes, 8-node hexahedra (ELFORM 2) of h = 0.5, 1, 1.5 and 3 mm. Parallel length ≈ 84 mm, fillet R ≈ 20 mm and grip width 26 mm were measured on the photo of the specimens (the data set does not give them). The width is reduced by 0.5 % at mid-length so the neck forms in the gauge length.

MAT_024 with the mean measured true stress–strain curve of Zx2–Zx4 up to A_g, then the generator's extension with slope H = σ_true(A_g). FAIL = k(h) · ln(1/(1 − Z)) with Z = 59 %, i.e. the value the MAT_024 generator writes for each element size.

Engineering strain = elongation of L0 / 60 mm; engineering stress = force / (6 × 20 mm²). After the force maximum the test curves are reconstructed from crosshead travel, so their end point is approximate (30–31.5 % instead of the measured A = 35 %).
Specimen pulled 28 mm in 70 ms (14 mm on the half model), with mass scaling to Δt = 5E-5 ms.
notes: With the measured curve up to A_g and the extension with slope H = σ_true(A_g), every mesh gives R_m = 509 MPa and A_g = 15.4–15.7 % (tests: R_m 504–519 MPa, A_g 14.9–15.5 %). The force maximum and the onset of necking do not depend on the element size.

With the generator's FAIL for each element size, the specimen breaks at A = 34.8–35.1 % for h = 0.5, 1, 1.5 and 3 mm, against A = 35 % in the test protocol. The same FAIL on a different mesh would not: FAIL = 1.0 breaks the 1 mm mesh at 34.9 % and the 0.5 mm mesh (FAIL 1.02) at 33.7 %, while on the 3 mm mesh already FAIL = 0.8 delays fracture to 37 %. Always pass the element size of the neck region to the generator (calibration runs in the MAT_024 documentation).

Between A_g and fracture the model carries more load than the test curves: 501–504 vs 489–502 MPa at 25 % strain, 483–493 vs 416–442 MPa at 30 %. Two effects add up. The test strain after the force maximum comes from crosshead travel and places fracture at 30–31.5 %, while the broken specimens measure A = 35 %, so the test branch is compressed along the strain axis. MAT_024 also has no damage softening before FAIL, whereas voids grow in the real neck. The model is therefore good for when the specimen breaks, less so for the shape of the load drop just before.

Fracture is abrupt in the model: the force drops to zero within one output interval, because MAT_024 deletes an element at FAIL without prior softening. To model the load drop itself, use the generator's GISSMO option (fracture model = 1, next example).

The calibration uses one steel and one specimen shape (uniaxial tension, thin plate). FAIL from Z describes fracture after necking in tension; under shear or high triaxiality (notches, thick plates, punching) the fracture strain differs, and a stress-state-dependent criterion is needed.

examples.title: S355 flat specimen — fracture with GISSMO instead of FAIL
setup: Same specimen, meshes and hardening curve as the example above, but with FAIL = 0 and the *MAT_ADD_DAMAGE_GISSMO card that the MAT_024 generator writes for Z = 59 % (fracture model = 1).

One card for all four meshes: failure strain in tension ε₀ = 1.219 for 1 mm elements, Rice–Tracey dependence on triaxiality, LCREGD factors 1.19 / 1.00 / 0.88 / 0.67 for h = 0.5 / 1 / 1.5 / 3 mm, ECRIT = plastic strain at A_g (0.139), DMGEXP = 2, FADEXP = 4.
Grey dashed lines: BAM tests Zx2–Zx4. The FAIL run on the 1 mm mesh from the example above is shown for comparison.
notes: With one GISSMO card for every mesh, the specimen breaks at A = 34.8–35.4 % for h = 1, 1.5 and 3 mm and at 34.0 % for h = 0.5 mm (test protocol: 35 %). R_m and A_g are the same as with FAIL (509 MPa, 15.4–15.7 %): ECRIT = plastic strain at A_g keeps damage from softening the material before necking.

The difference from FAIL is the end of the curve. With FAIL the stress stays at 450–480 MPa up to 34 % and then falls to zero within about 1 % strain. With GISSMO the stress starts to fall at about 31 % and goes from about 450 MPa at 32 % to 50–90 MPa at 34–34.5 %: the crack grows across the width over about 3 % strain instead of the whole neck eroding at once.

The tests drop earlier and more steeply (416–442 MPa at 30 % against 480–484 MPa in the model). Part of this is the test strain axis after the force maximum, which comes from crosshead travel and ends at 30–31.5 % although the broken specimens measure A = 35 %. GISSMO with FADEXP = 4 was chosen to reproduce a drop to about 0.85 R_m before the final break, not the test curve point by point.

FAIL is written for one element size (the h input), so it suits a uniform mesh in the neck. GISSMO takes the element size from the mesh (LCREGD), so a model with fine elements in the connection and coarse elements elsewhere keeps one material card. The factors were calibrated for 8-node solids in tension; shells and shear-dominated fracture need their own calibration (see the MAT_024 documentation).

examples.title: S355 flat specimen — hardening beyond A_g: flat tail vs. slope at the Considère criterion
setup: Same BAM S355 specimen, one-eighth model and tests as in the two examples above. The measured true stress–strain curve up to A_g (plastic strain 0.139, true stress 586 MPa) is continued in two ways: with slope H = σ_true(A_g), the generator default, at which the Considère criterion dσ/dε = σ is met at A_g; or flat (H = 0), as many hand-made curves end and as the generator did up to version 1.1.

Runs without a fracture model show the neck alone (1 mm mesh). Runs with FAIL use the generator values for Z = 59 %: 1.150, 1.008 and 0.722 for h = 0.5, 1 and 3 mm, which were calibrated with H = σ_true(A_g).
Z at 20 % elongation is the reduction of the mid-length cross-section, read from the deformed model.
Grey dashed lines: BAM tests Zx2–Zx4.

inputChart.title: Input: hardening curve LCSS (what LS-DYNA reads)
inputChart.caption: Both curves are the measured true curve up to A_g (plastic strain 0.139, 586 MPa); they differ only beyond it. Flat tail: the last point repeats 586 MPa at plastic strain 2.0, so the steel stops hardening at A_g. Slope at the Considère criterion: a straight line with slope dσ/dε_p = σ_true(A_g) = 586 MPa per unit plastic strain, reaching 1676 MPa at plastic strain 2.0. That end point is never reached: the neck breaks at plastic strains of about 1 (FAIL = 1.01 for 1 mm elements); it only fixes the slope. LS-DYNA interpolates linearly between the points.

runs.label: H = σ(A_g), no fracture, h = 1 mm
flat tail, no fracture, h = 1 mm

notes: Up to the force maximum the two curves are the same material: R_m = 508.2–508.6 MPa in every run (tests 504–519 MPa). The flat tail lets the neck start a little earlier, A_g = 14.0–14.2 % against 15.4 % (tests 14.9–15.5 %).

Without a fracture model the difference is the neck itself. With H = σ_true(A_g) the specimen still carries 508 MPa at 20 % elongation with Z = 23 %, and 482 MPa with Z = 49 % at 30 %; the neck is long and diffuse (peak plastic strain 0.69 at 30 %, see the plots). With the flat tail the load falls to 389 MPa with Z = 42 % at 20 %, and to 152 MPa with Z = 97 % at 30 %: the strain concentrates in a crossed band (peak plastic strain 2.3) and the neck collapses. The curve is shown up to 31 %; after that the collapsed elements make the force noisy and the run stops at 33 % (error termination for excessive mass scaling).

With the same FAIL values the flat tail breaks the specimen at A = 24.0, 24.6 and 24.5 % for h = 0.5, 1 and 3 mm, against 34.9 % with H = σ_true(A_g) (35.1 / 34.8 % for 0.5 / 3 mm) and 35 % in the tests. FAIL is reached about 10 points of elongation too early because the neck thins much faster, not because of the element size: A hardly changes with the mesh in either case, since FAIL is scaled with h.

Why the flat tail is wrong: after the force maximum the engineering stress falls because the section shrinks, but the true stress of steel keeps rising up to fracture. A flat true curve says the steel stops hardening exactly at A_g, so nothing slows the neck down. With a slope equal to σ_true(A_g) the Considère criterion places the onset of necking exactly at A_g, and the hardening that continues beyond it lets the neck grow gradually, as in the tests.

In practice: never end a MAT_024 curve at R_m or A_g with a flat line. Continue it to plastic strains well above the fracture strain (the generator adds 2.0), and calibrate FAIL or GISSMO together with that extension, because the fracture strain only makes sense for one post-necking curve.

examples.title: Open-data benchmark 1 — cylinder 75 × 150 mm, f_c = 55.6 MPa (Hoover et al. 2013)
setup: A blind check of the generators against published tests: one concrete batch (d_max = 10 mm, w/c 0.41) tested as cylinders and as notched beams of several sizes. This example and the next two use the cylinders and the D = 93 and 215 mm beams.

Every card is the site's generator output for f_c = 55.6 MPa (measured mean of the 75 × 150 mm cylinders at 400 days) and d_max = 10 mm; nothing was fitted to these tests. KCC runs with LCRATE = 0 and is regularised for each mesh (h input = element size).

MAT_172 works only with shells and beams, so its run is a 75 × 150 mm plane-stress strip of 3.75 mm shells (ELFORM 16) whose thickness, 58.9 mm, gives the cylinder's cross-section area; its card is the generator output (version 1.1) for f_c = 55.6 MPa, h = 3.75 mm, TYPEC = 9.

Full cylinder, O-grid mesh of 16 000 hexahedra (3.75 mm), ELFORM 1 with IHQ 4 / QM 0.05. Frictionless platens; top face pushed down 0.75 mm (5 ‰) in 30 ms. Stress = bottom reaction / (π · 37.5²), strain = platen displacement / 150 mm.

Test data: Hoover, Bažant, Vorel, Wendner, Hubler, Eng. Fract. Mech. 114 (2013) 92–103, doi:10.1016/j.engfracmech.2013.08.007, and Wendner et al., Mater. Struct. 48 (2015) 3603–3626, doi:10.1617/s11527-014-0426-0; curves from the ConcreteTestCollection that BOKU Vienna publishes for model calibration. Grey dashed line: measured mean curve; its min/max envelopes snap back after the peak and are left out.
notes: The peak is not a validation, because f_c is the input: KCC, Winfrith, CSCM and CDP peak at 55.6, 56.8, 54.6 and 53.0 MPa (−5 to +2 %). What the test checks is the rest of the curve.

Stiffness. The test rises almost linearly with about 34 GPa (6.5 MPa at 0.19 ‰; the paper reports E_cyl = 34.4 GPa). Winfrith and CSCM start at 37.8 GPa, CDP at 35.2 GPa and KCC at 35.4 GPa, close to the E = 35.3–38.1 GPa their generators derive from f_c. Before generator version 1.5 the KCC EOS was not scaled with f_c and this card started at 31.4 GPa.

Shape before the peak. The test peaks at 1.76 ‰ and rounds off from about 45 MPa. Winfrith and CSCM stay linear up to about 1.45 ‰ and then run flat (54–57 MPa) like an elastic–perfectly plastic material, so their peak strains in the table (2.8 and 5 ‰) are just points on that plateau. KCC and CDP round off and peak at 2.0 and 2.3 ‰.

Post-peak. The measured mean curve snaps back (the strain decreases while the load falls), which a displacement-controlled model with uniform strain cannot follow. Only CDP softens (40.5 MPa at 4.9 ‰); KCC, Winfrith and CSCM stay at 54–57 MPa up to 5 ‰. For KCC part of this comes from the regularisation: the generator stretches the whole λ–η softening branch to the element size, so a 3.75 mm element also softens slowly in compression.

Hourglass energy is below 0.3 % and kinetic energy below 0.03 % of the external work for all four models. No fringe images are shown: with frictionless platens the field stays uniform up to 5 ‰, so the pictures carry no information.

MAT_172 (EC2, shell strip, generator 1.1) starts at 36.6 GPa (E_cm = 36.8 GPa from EN 1992-1-1, Table 3.1, against 34.4 GPa measured) and follows the EC2 curve to 55.6 MPa at 2.43 ‰. Right after the peak the stress drops in steps (about 21 MPa at 2.5–2.9 ‰, 7 MPa at 3.0–3.5 ‰, 2.4 MPa at 5 ‰): between ε_c1 and ε_cu1 = 3.5 ‰ the EC2 curve falls by a third over 1 ‰ of strain, so one row of 3.75 mm elements after the other softens faster than the rest of the 150 mm strip unloads (a snap-back, as in the measured curve). Beyond ε_cu1 the generator's ECSP69 spreads the remaining softening over G_c = 100 G_F; kinetic energy stays below 0.01 % of the work. With generator 1.0 (default ECSP69) the stress went to zero and the crushed strip flew apart (kinetic energy 27 %).

examples.title: Open-data benchmark 2 — notched beam D = 93 mm, three-point bending (Hoover et al. 2013)
setup: Beam D = 93 mm, thickness 40 mm, span 202 mm (2.176 D), central notch 27 mm deep (a/D = 0.29 on the 3 mm grid; test 0.3) and one element wide. 30 108 hexahedra of 3 mm, ELFORM 2.

Every card is the site's generator output for f_c = 55.6 MPa (measured mean of the 75 × 150 mm cylinders at 400 days) and d_max = 10 mm; nothing was fitted to these tests. KCC runs with LCRATE = 0 and is regularised for each mesh (h input = element size).

MAT_172 works only with shells and beams, so its run is a plane-stress shell model in the vertical plane with the same element size, supports and loading (ELFORM 16, thickness = beam width 40 mm); its card is the generator output (version 1.1) for f_c = 55.6 MPa with h = element size, TYPEC = 9, d_max left blank (plain concrete).

Supports and load line are rows of nodes (three node lines at each support, two at midspan); midspan pushed down 0.45 mm in 30 ms. Load = sum of the support reactions; deflection = mean of the two top nodes at midspan.

Work / ligament = area under the load–deflection curve up to the end of the run, divided by 40 × (D − a). The same integral of the measured mean curve (to 0.43 mm) is 0.126 N/mm; the paper's work-of-fracture G_F of this concrete is 0.097–0.111 N/mm.

Test data: Hoover, Bažant, Vorel, Wendner, Hubler, Eng. Fract. Mech. 114 (2013) 92–103, doi:10.1016/j.engfracmech.2013.08.007, and Wendner et al., Mater. Struct. 48 (2015) 3603–3626, doi:10.1617/s11527-014-0426-0; curves from the ConcreteTestCollection that BOKU Vienna publishes for model calibration. Grey dashed lines: measured mean curve and its min/max envelope.
notes: Peak load (test mean 3.46 kN): KCC 3.39 kN (−2 %), Winfrith 3.89 (+13 %), CSCM 3.99 (+15 %), CDP 3.71 (+7 %). The models peak at 0.030–0.035 mm deflection, the test at 0.024 mm.

Softening. At 0.1 mm the test carries 1.08 kN; KCC 1.22, CSCM 0.89, Winfrith 0.60 and CDP 1.63 kN, and at 0.2 mm 0.41 kN against KCC 0.36 and CDP 0.51 kN. KCC follows the measured tail most closely, Winfrith and CSCM drop too fast just after the peak, and CDP stays above the test up to about 0.25 mm.

Energy against the input. CDP dissipates 0.151 N/mm, the area of its bilinear card (0.150 N/mm, the fib MC2010 G_F = 73 f_cm^0.18). That is 35–55 % above the measured G_F of this concrete; Hoover et al. note that the fib formula overestimates it by about 50 %. KCC targets the same fib value and dissipates 0.130 N/mm, close to the 0.126 N/mm of the test curve. Winfrith and CSCM start from the lower MC90 value (0.088 N/mm) and dissipate 0.110 and 0.124 N/mm.
Hourglass energy is zero except for Winfrith (6.4 %, one-point element only); kinetic energy is below 0.15 % of the work.

In the fringe plots the crack runs straight up from the notch in all four models; CSCM erodes it (white gap). KCC and CSCM also show local crushing over the supports, which are rows of fixed nodes without bearing plates.

MAT_172 (EC2, plane-stress shells, generator 1.1) peaks at 3.93 kN (+14 %), like Winfrith and CSCM, and softens more slowly than the test: 1.93 kN at 0.1 mm (test 1.08) and 0.63 kN at 0.2 mm (test 0.40). It dissipates 0.178 N/mm, 18 % above its card's G_F (0.150 N/mm). Checks on this beam: with the measured G_F of this concrete (0.104 N/mm, mean of the paper's 0.097–0.111) instead of the fib estimate the peak is 3.64 kN (+5 %) and the load 1.21 kN at 0.1 mm, so most of the excess comes from the fib G_F, which Hoover et al. note is about 50 % too high for this concrete. Splitting the beam into parts shows that about a quarter of the energy is dissipated by local cracking at the loaded node and the support nodes, not in the main crack. The 2-crack option (TYPEC = 109), half the loading rate and a 1.5 mm mesh (3.70 kN, 0.187 N/mm) change little. Hourglass energy is zero (fully integrated shells).

examples.title: Open-data benchmark 3 — notched beam D = 215 mm and the size effect (Hoover et al. 2013)
setup: Beam D = 215 mm, thickness 40 mm, span 469 mm, notch 65 mm (a/D = 0.30), one element wide. 36 016 hexahedra of 5 mm, ELFORM 2; midspan pushed down 0.9 mm in 40 ms. Load, deflection and work / ligament as in the D = 93 mm example (measured mean curve: 0.138 N/mm to 0.55 mm).

Every card is the site's generator output for f_c = 55.6 MPa (measured mean of the 75 × 150 mm cylinders at 400 days) and d_max = 10 mm; nothing was fitted to these tests. KCC runs with LCRATE = 0 and is regularised for each mesh (h input = element size).

MAT_172 works only with shells and beams, so its run is a plane-stress shell model in the vertical plane with the same element size, supports and loading (ELFORM 16, thickness = beam width 40 mm); its card is the generator output (version 1.1) for f_c = 55.6 MPa with h = element size, TYPEC = 9, d_max left blank (plain concrete).
Same cards as for D = 93 mm except KCC, which the generator regularises for 5 mm instead of 3 mm elements.

Test data: Hoover, Bažant, Vorel, Wendner, Hubler, Eng. Fract. Mech. 114 (2013) 92–103, doi:10.1016/j.engfracmech.2013.08.007, and Wendner et al., Mater. Struct. 48 (2015) 3603–3626, doi:10.1617/s11527-014-0426-0; curves from the ConcreteTestCollection that BOKU Vienna publishes for model calibration. Grey dashed lines: measured mean curve and its min/max envelope.
notes: Peak load (test mean 6.57 kN): KCC 6.72 kN (+2 %), Winfrith 7.14 (+9 %), CSCM 7.34 (+12 %), CDP 6.83 (+4 %).

Size effect. The nominal strength σ_N = 1.5 P S / (W D²) falls from 3.03 to 2.50 MPa between D = 93 and 215 mm, a ratio of 0.826. The models give 0.860 (KCC), 0.797 (Winfrith), 0.800 (CSCM) and 0.799 (CDP): all four reproduce the size effect within 4 % from the generator cards alone.

KCC up to generator version 1.5 was 19 % low in both sizes. The cause was the tensile damage law, not the inputs: one element with the same card reaches its tensile strength in uniaxial, plane-strain and biaxial tension and dissipates the target G_F in uniaxial tension. In the beam, a cracked KCC element is left in near-hydrostatic tension (σxx ≈ σyy ≈ σzz ≈ 2.8 MPa) because the crack opening goes into elastic volumetric strain that the surrounding concrete does not let it relieve, and KCC's damage grows with (1 + p/f_t)^−b2. With the K&C value b2 = 1.86 each cracked element dissipated about 0.08 instead of 0.15 N/mm. Since version 1.6 the generator writes b2 = 1.0 and re-stretches λ so that uniaxial tension still dissipates G_F: the beams now peak at 3.39 and 6.72 kN (−2 and +2 %) and dissipate 0.130 and 0.144 N/mm. Other changes tried on the D = 93 mm beam did not help: ω = 0 / 0.9 / 1.0 gave 2.60 / 3.79 / 6.13 kN with no softening left from ω = 0.9 on, b3 had no effect, steel bearing pads added 4 %, and scaling the EOS with f_c (version 1.5) 1–3 %. b2 = 1.0 was chosen so that the beams dissipate the card's G_F, on this one data set (f_c = 55.6 MPa).

Energy. CDP again dissipates its card value (0.153 N/mm), about 40 % above the paper's G_F; KCC 0.144, CSCM 0.126 and Winfrith 0.165 N/mm. When a fracture test of the concrete is available, scale CDP's WF and WF1 (or KCC's gf input) to the measured G_F instead of using the fib estimate.
Hourglass energy is zero except for Winfrith (7.1 %); kinetic energy is below 0.7 % of the work.
MAT_172 (EC2, plane-stress shells, generator 1.1) peaks at 7.28 kN (+11 %) and dissipates 0.220 N/mm (card: 0.150 N/mm). Its size-effect ratio σ_N(215)/σ_N(93) is 0.804 (test 0.826).

examples.title: Open-data benchmark 4 — reinforced concrete panels in pure shear (Vecchio & Collins 1986), MAT_172
setup: Twelve of the 30 panels of Vecchio & Collins (1986): 890 × 890 × 70 mm, two layers of welded wire mesh, d_max = 6 mm, loaded through shear keys in monotonic pure shear. Kept: every panel loaded 1:0:0 that did not fail at the edges, was not precracked or poorly cast and did not fail by wire fracture (PV4, PV6, PV10–PV13, PV16, PV19–PV22, PV27). f_c 14.5–29.8 MPa, ρ_x 0.74–1.79 %, ρ_y 0–1.79 %.

The stress field in the tests is uniform, so each panel is one 50 × 50 mm shell (ELFORM 16) with a *PART_COMPOSITE section: concrete / x-steel layer (t = ρ_x · 70 mm) / y-steel layer / concrete. All three cards are generator output (version 1.1) for the panel's f_c with h = 50 mm and d_max = 6 mm; the steel layers use rho = 100 % in one direction and that direction's measured f_y (MAT_172 has one yield stress per card). E_s = 200 GPa (not given in the paper).

Load control as in the test: self-equilibrated nodal shear forces ramped to 1.5 v_u(test) in 60 ms on a statically determinate support. v_u (model) = largest shear stress in the element before the shear strain exceeds 50 ‰ (after failure it grows by orders of magnitude).

Test data: Vecchio, F. J., & Collins, M. P. (1986). The modified compression-field theory for reinforced concrete elements subjected to shear. ACI Journal, 83(2), 219–231, doi:10.14359/10416, Table 1 (also in tools/examples/data/vecchio_collins_1986_panels.csv).
notes: Generator 1.0 cards gave a mean of 0.94 with CoV 19 % (0.64–1.25). Two options of MAT_172 made the difference, both switched on in version 1.1. AGGSZ = d_max (NS 3473 aggregate interlock) raised the panels with little transverse steel, whose strength after the y-steel yields depends on shear transfer across the fixed cracks: PV12 0.64 → 0.80, PV13 0.76 → 0.97, PV19 0.76 → 0.89. DEGRAD = 1 reduces the compressive strength parallel to open cracks and lowered the heavily reinforced panels that fail by crushing: PV27 1.25 → 1.16. Its formula, 1/(0.8 + 100 ε_t,max), has the same form as the compression softening Vecchio & Collins derived from these tests, 1/(0.8 − 0.34 ε_1/ε'_c).

Remaining errors follow the fixed-crack limitation of MAT_172: the panels with the least transverse steel are still 11–20 % low, and the crushing-governed panels with the most steel (PV22, PV27) 14–16 % high.

AGGSZ is not written by default: on the plain-concrete Hoover beams it adds shear transfer that spreads cracking to the neighbouring columns of elements and raises the post-peak energy by about 30 %. Enter d_max for reinforced members in shear.

The panels check strength only (one element, no localisation). The model cracks at v ≈ f_ctm, 1.1–2.3 MPa: 11 and 15 % above the test for PV4 and PV6 (f_c 26.6 and 29.8 MPa), 17–40 % below it for the ten panels with f_c ≤ 21.7 MPa (PV10: 1.11 against 1.86 MPa). Below f_c = 20 MPa, f_ck = f_cm − 8 MPa falls under C12 and the EN 1992-1-1 formula for f_ctm is extrapolated.

examples.title: Open-data benchmark 5 — perforation of a 178 mm slab by an ogive-nose projectile (Hanchak et al. 1992)
setup: Hanchak et al. (1992), 48 MPa concrete: 610 × 610 × 178 mm slabs, 2440 kg/m³, d_max 9.5 mm, three rebar mats. Projectile: 0.50 kg steel, Ø 25.4 mm, 3.0 CRH ogive nose. Eight shots, V_s 301–1058 m/s, residual velocity V_r measured (Table 2). Shot 1-0058 struck the rebar; the authors saw no effect on V_r, and the rebar is not modelled.

Quarter model, rigid projectile with axial motion only, 5 hexahedra over the projectile radius along the path (2.54 mm), graded outward; frictionless *CONTACT_ERODING_SURFACE_TO_SURFACE, SFS = SFM = 100. Concrete cards are generator output for f_c = 48 MPa with the measured density; each model's own erosion is switched off.

Erosion: one criterion for all models, *MAT_ADD_EROSION on the maximum principal strain MXEPS, plus deletion of any element whose time step falls below 1 % of the initial one (*CONTROL_TERMINATION DTMIN = 0.01, *CONTROL_TIMESTEP ERODE = 1). MXEPS is calibrated per model on shot 1-0054 (V_s 749, V_r 615 m/s) and the other seven shots are predictions.

Test data: Hanchak, S. J., Forrestal, M. J., Young, E. R., Ehrgott, J. Q. (1992). Perforation of concrete slabs with 48 MPa (7 ksi) and 140 MPa (20 ksi) unconfined compressive strengths. International Journal of Impact Engineering 12(1), 1–7, doi:10.1016/0734-743X(92)90282-X (also in tools/examples/data/penetration_tests.csv). Builder: tools/examples/build_penetration.py; the deck in each row is shot 1-0054.
notes: Above 600 m/s the calibrated models predict V_r within 8 % (KCC 896, RHT 923, Winfrith 995, CSCM 981 m/s against 947 m/s at V_s 1058), except Winfrith at 606 m/s (341 against 449 m/s, −24 %).

Near the ballistic limit KCC, RHT and CSCM are too weak: at V_s 301 m/s the test projectile stopped, the models exit at 101–168 m/s, and at 360–434 m/s V_r is 55–160 m/s above the test. Winfrith is the opposite: it stops the projectile at 301 and 360 m/s but is too strong up to 606 m/s (V_r 18 against 136 m/s at 381 m/s).

One MXEPS cannot fit the whole V_s–V_r curve: a larger MXEPS makes the slab stronger at every velocity, so moving the low-velocity points onto the test moves the calibration shot off it. The same trend (models too weak near the ballistic limit) is reported by Kwak & Gang (2015, doi:10.1016/j.ijimpeng.2015.07.008) and Islam et al. (2011, doi:10.12989/cac.2011.8.1.111).

Mesh: on shot 1-0068 (V_s 301 m/s, MXEPS 0.5) refining the path elements from 5.1 to 2.54 mm raised V_r from 9 to 124 m/s with RHT; results are not mesh converged, and the calibrated MXEPS belongs to the 2.54 mm mesh.

Use: a calibrated eroding Lagrangian model is a reasonable estimate of V_r well above the ballistic limit (here V_s ≥ 600 m/s, about twice V_bl); it should not be used to predict the ballistic limit itself.
